summary:
Our project, the "Mars Outpost Trade-off Simulator," is an interactive, physics-based educational tool designed to bridge the gap between complex aerospace engineering and STEM education. We developed a web application using Python and Streamlit that allows junior astronauts to manage a Martian outpost.
To address the challenge, our simulator does not rely on arbitrary game mechanics; instead, it integrates real-world physical constraints. Players must balance power generation, life support mass, and radiation shielding. The underlying engine utilizes the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation to calculate payload limits and Mars solar irradiance data to determine power output.
This project is important because it transforms abstract orbital mechanics and thermodynamic trade-offs into a tangible, engaging experience. It teaches future explorers that in space mission design, every resource added requires a critical compromise in mass and energy.
details:
How it works & Factors considered:
Our simulator operates on a rigorous physics engine. When users adjust parameters like "Solar Panel Area" or "Radiation Shielding Thickness," the system calculates the outcomes based on aerospace principles:

  1. Orbital Mechanics & Mass Constraints: We applied the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation to set a strict Initial Mass in Low Earth Orbit (IMLEO) limit. Adding heavy radiation shielding reduces the available mass for life support.
  2. Power Generation: We utilized the Martian solar irradiance constant (
    Gmars≈590 W/m2Gmars​≈590 W/m2
    ) to calculate realistic power outputs:
    P = A ⋅ η ⋅ Gmars⋅cos⁡(θ)P=A⋅η⋅Gmars​⋅cos(θ)
    .
  3. Radiation Shielding: We incorporated basic mass attenuation concepts to simulate the trade-off between crew safety from Solar Particle Events (SPEs) and launch mass.

Tools & Creativity:
We used Python for the numerical calculations and the Streamlit library to create an intuitive, low-code web interface. Our creativity lies in "gamifying" hard physics. Instead of oversimplifying space travel, we force young learners to face the exact same mass-to-power dilemmas that NASA's GNC and systems engineers face today.
